q: Which statement about a redox reaction is correct?
o: Oxidation takes place without any reduction
Reduction always happens before oxidation is complete
Only non-metals take part in it
Oxidation and reduction take place at the same time
x: Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another, so oxidation and reduction always occur together. That is why the reaction is called redox.

q: In any electrochemical cell, the anode is the electrode at which:
x: Oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, in both galvanic and electrolytic cells.

q: In an electrolytic cell, the anode is:
o: Connected to the negative terminal of the battery, and oxidation occurs there
Connected to the positive terminal of the battery, and oxidation occurs there
Connected to the positive terminal of the battery, and reduction occurs there
Connected to the negative terminal of the battery, and reduction occurs there
x: In electrolysis the anode is joined to the positive terminal, so it attracts anions, which lose electrons (oxidation). The cathode is negative and reduction occurs there.

q: In terms of electrons, oxidation is defined as:
x: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons. Gaining protons has nothing to do with this definition.

q: In a galvanic cell such as the Daniell cell, the cathode is:
o: The negative electrode, where reduction takes place
The positive electrode, where oxidation takes place
The positive electrode, where reduction takes place
The negative electrode, where oxidation takes place
x: In a galvanic cell electrons arrive at the cathode, where Cu²⁺ is reduced; this electrode is positive. In an electrolytic cell the cathode is the negative electrode, but reduction still occurs there.

q: Which of the following is NOT a redox reaction?
x: In the neutralisation, Na stays +1, O −2, H +1 and Cl −1, so no oxidation number changes. In the other three, a free element becomes combined, so oxidation numbers change.

q: In the Daniell cell (Zn in ZnSO₄, Cu in CuSO₄), electrons flow through the external wire:
o: From the copper electrode to the zinc electrode
Through the salt bridge from zinc to copper
From the zinc electrode to the copper electrode
x: Zinc is oxidised at the anode and releases electrons, which travel through the wire to the copper cathode where Cu²⁺ is reduced. Ions, not electrons, move through the salt bridge.

q: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, electrons are transferred:
o: From copper(II) ions to zinc atoms
From zinc atoms to the sulphate ions
From zinc atoms to copper(II) ions
From water molecules to zinc atoms
x: Zn loses 2 electrons to become Zn²⁺ (oxidation) and Cu²⁺ gains them to become Cu (reduction). Sulphate ions are spectators.

q: Electrode potential is the:
o: Current that flows through an electrolyte during electrolysis
Mass of metal deposited on an electrode
Energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom
Potential difference set up between a metal and a solution of its own ions
x: When a metal dips into a solution of its ions, an equilibrium is set up and a potential difference develops between them; this is the electrode potential. The last option describes ionisation energy.

q: In any balanced redox reaction, the total number of electrons lost by the reducing agent is:
o: Always greater than the number gained by the oxidising agent
Equal to the total number gained by the oxidising agent
Always less than the number gained by the oxidising agent
Unrelated to the number gained by the oxidising agent
x: Electrons cannot be created or destroyed, so those lost in oxidation must equal those gained in reduction. This is the basis for balancing redox equations.

q: The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) consists of:
o: A copper rod dipped in 1 mol dm⁻³ CuSO₄, with H₂ gas bubbled over it
Platinum in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ HCl, with O₂ gas bubbled over it
A zinc rod dipped in 1 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄
Platinum coated with platinum black in 1 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, with H₂ gas bubbled over it at standard pressure
x: The SHE is a platinised platinum electrode in a 1 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ solution with pure hydrogen at standard pressure and 25 °C. The other set-ups lack H⁺ at unit concentration or hydrogen gas.

q: Which change is an oxidation?
x: H₂S losing hydrogen to form S is oxidation; sulphur goes from −2 to 0. The other three are reductions: loss of oxygen, gain of an electron, and a fall in charge.

q: By convention, the standard electrode potential of the standard hydrogen electrode is taken as:
x: The SHE is the reference electrode and is assigned 0.00 V. −0.76 V and +0.34 V are the standard potentials of the zinc and copper electrodes.

q: In Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, what happens to chlorine?
o: It is both oxidised (to +1) and reduced (to −1)
It is only oxidised, from 0 to +1
It is only reduced, from 0 to −1
It is neither oxidised nor reduced
x: Chlorine starts at 0. In NaCl it is −1 (reduced) and in NaClO it is +1 (oxidised). A reaction in which one element is both oxidised and reduced is called disproportionation.

q: Platinum is used as the metal in the standard hydrogen electrode because it:
o: Reacts with H⁺ ions to produce hydrogen gas
Has the most negative electrode potential of all metals
Is inert and conducts electrons, and its platinum black coating adsorbs hydrogen
Is oxidised to Pt²⁺ ions, which supply the electrons
x: Platinum takes no part in the reaction; it only provides a conducting surface. The finely divided platinum black gives a large surface that adsorbs hydrogen so the H₂/H⁺ equilibrium is set up quickly.

q: Which of the following decomposition reactions is a redox reaction?
x: In 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂, mercury goes from +2 to 0 and oxygen from −2 to 0. In the other three no oxidation number changes.

q: The function of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell is to:
o: Carry electrons from the anode to the cathode
Supply the metal ions that are deposited at the cathode
Complete the circuit and keep both solutions electrically neutral
Prevent any reaction from taking place at the anode
x: Ions move through the salt bridge to balance the charge building up in each half-cell, which completes the circuit. Electrons travel through the external wire, not the bridge.

q: For the reaction Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂, the oxidation half-reaction is:
x: Magnesium loses two electrons, so its half-reaction is the oxidation: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ is the reduction half-reaction.

q: Why is the potential of an electrode always measured by connecting it to a standard hydrogen electrode?
o: The potential of a single electrode cannot be measured on its own; only a difference between two electrodes can
The SHE supplies the electrons needed by every electrode
Hydrogen is the most reactive element, so it gives the largest reading
The SHE makes the electrode react faster
x: A voltmeter measures only the potential difference between two electrodes. So a reference electrode with an agreed value of 0.00 V, the SHE, is used and the measured cell voltage gives the electrode's potential.

q: How many electrons are transferred in the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + Sn²⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + Sn⁴⁺ as written?
x: Sn²⁺ → Sn⁴⁺ loses 2 electrons; each Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺ gains 1, and there are 2 Fe³⁺. So 2 electrons are transferred in total.

q: A current of 2.0 A is passed through aqueous CuSO₄ for 965 s. What mass of copper is deposited at the cathode? (Cu = 63.5, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
x: Q = It = 2.0 × 965 = 1930 C = 0.02 F. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 0.02 F deposits 0.01 mol Cu = 0.635 g. Forgetting that each Cu²⁺ needs 2 electrons gives 1.27 g.

q: In the electrolysis of molten Al₂O₃, a steady current of 9.65 A is used. How long does it take to deposit 0.27 g of aluminium? (Al = 27, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
x: 0.27 g Al = 0.01 mol; Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al needs 0.03 F = 2895 C. t = Q/I = 2895/9.65 = 300 s. Taking one electron per Al atom gives the tempting 100 s.

q: Two cells, one with aqueous AgNO₃ and one with aqueous CuSO₄, are connected in series. When 4.32 g of silver is deposited in the first cell, what mass of copper is deposited in the second? (Ag = 108, Cu = 63.5)
x: Series cells pass the same charge. 4.32/108 = 0.04 mol Ag = 0.04 F; Cu²⁺ needs 2 F per mol, so 0.02 mol Cu = 1.27 g. Ignoring the 1:2 electron ratio (one mole of Cu per mole of Ag) gives 2.54 g.

q: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine) is electrolysed with inert electrodes. The main products at the electrodes are:
o: Na at the cathode and Cl₂ at the anode
H₂ at the cathode and Cl₂ at the anode
H₂ at the cathode and O₂ at the anode
Cl₂ at the cathode and H₂ at the anode
x: At the cathode water is reduced more easily than Na⁺, giving H₂ (and OH⁻); in concentrated brine Cl⁻ is oxidised at the anode to Cl₂. Sodium metal forms only from molten NaCl, the most tempting slip.

q: Aqueous CuSO₄ is electrolysed using copper electrodes. Which change takes place at the anode?
o: Oxygen gas is evolved and the solution becomes acidic
Copper atoms are oxidised to Cu²⁺ ions and the anode loses mass
Cu²⁺ ions are reduced and copper is deposited on the anode
Sulphate ions are oxidised to sulphur dioxide
x: A copper anode is oxidised itself, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, more easily than water, so it dissolves while copper deposits at the cathode and [Cu²⁺] stays constant. Oxygen evolution is what happens with inert (platinum) electrodes.

q: One faraday (about 96500 C) is the quantity of electricity carried by:
o: One gram-equivalent of hydrogen gas at STP
x: The Faraday constant is the charge on one mole of electrons, Nₐ × e ≈ 96500 C. One mole of a doubly charged ion carries 2 F, so 'one mole of any ion' is the tempting slip.

q: The Faraday constant is 96500 C mol⁻¹ and the charge on one electron is 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What value of the Avogadro constant follows from these?
x: F = Nₐ × e, so Nₐ = 96500 / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.03 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 1.54 × 10⁻¹⁴.

q: 0.2 F of electricity is passed through aqueous Na₂SO₄ using platinum electrodes. What is the total volume of gas (both electrodes together) collected at STP? (molar volume 22.4 dm³)
x: Water is electrolysed: cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻ gives 0.1 mol H₂; anode 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ gives 0.05 mol O₂. Total 0.15 mol × 22.4 = 3.36 dm³. Counting only the hydrogen gives 2.24 dm³.

q: A steel spoon is to be electroplated with silver. Which arrangement is correct?
o: Spoon as anode, silver plate as cathode, a silver salt solution as electrolyte
Spoon as cathode, silver plate as anode, an iron salt solution as electrolyte
Spoon as anode, graphite as cathode, a silver salt solution as electrolyte
Spoon as cathode, silver plate as anode, a silver salt solution as electrolyte
x: Ag⁺ ions are reduced and deposited on the object, so the spoon must be the cathode; the silver anode dissolves to replace the Ag⁺ used. Swapping the electrodes (spoon as anode) is the usual slip: the spoon would then corrode.

q: Given E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = −2.37 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, what is the standard emf of the cell made from these two electrodes?
x: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.80 − (−2.37) = 3.17 V; silver is the cathode. Electrode potentials are not multiplied by the 2 in 2Ag⁺ + 2e⁻, so doubling 0.80 to get 3.97 V is wrong; 1.57 V comes from ignoring the minus sign of Mg.

q: In a lead storage battery (lead accumulator) that is supplying current, the anode is made of:
x: During discharge Pb is oxidised at the anode, Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻, while PbO₂ is reduced at the cathode. Choosing PbO₂ mixes up the anode and cathode.

q: As a lead storage battery discharges, the density of its sulphuric acid electrolyte:
o: Increases, because water is used up at both plates
Stays the same, because the acid acts only as a conductor
Decreases, because H₂SO₄ is used up and water is formed
Increases, because PbSO₄ dissolves in the acid
x: Overall Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O, so the acid is consumed and diluted; its density falls, which is why a hydrometer shows the state of charge. The PbSO₄ formed is insoluble and stays on the plates.

q: In a rechargeable nickel–cadmium cell, the anode during discharge is:
x: In the Ni–Cd cell cadmium is oxidised at the anode, Cd + 2OH⁻ → Cd(OH)₂ + 2e⁻, and the nickel oxide is reduced at the cathode; KOH is the electrolyte. Zinc is the anode of dry cells, not of this cell.

q: In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with aqueous KOH as the electrolyte, which reaction takes place at the anode?
x: Hydrogen is the fuel and is oxidised at the anode; in alkaline electrolyte it combines with OH⁻ to form water. O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ is a reduction, the cathode reaction, and is the tempting mix-up.

q: In a zinc–carbon dry cell (Leclanché type), the anode is:
x: Zinc is oxidised, Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻, so the zinc case is the anode (negative terminal). The carbon rod surrounded by MnO₂ is the cathode where reduction occurs; picking it confuses the positive terminal with the anode.

q: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V. Using the Nernst equation E = E° + (0.0591/n) log [Zn²⁺], what is the electrode potential of zinc in 0.01 mol dm⁻³ Zn²⁺ at 25 °C?
x: n = 2 and log 0.01 = −2, so E = −0.76 + (0.0591/2)(−2) = −0.76 − 0.059 = −0.82 V. Forgetting to divide by n = 2 gives −0.88 V; a sign slip gives −0.70 V.

q: For the cell Zn | Zn²⁺(0.1 mol dm⁻³) || Cu²⁺(1.0 mol dm⁻³) | Cu, E°cell = 1.10 V. Using Ecell = E°cell − (0.0591/n) log ([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]), the emf at 25 °C is about:
x: Two electrons are transferred, so Ecell = 1.10 − 0.02955 × log(0.1/1) = 1.10 + 0.03 = 1.13 V. Lowering [Zn²⁺] favours the forward reaction, so the emf rises. A sign slip gives 1.07 V; using n = 1 gives 1.16 V.

q: A hydrogen electrode (H₂ at 1 atm) dips into a solution of pH 3 at 25 °C. Using the Nernst equation, its reduction potential is about: (E° = 0.00 V; E = −0.0591 × pH for this electrode)
x: For 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, E = 0.00 + 0.0591 log [H⁺] = −0.0591 × 3 = −0.18 V; less H⁺ than standard makes the potential negative. Halving again for n = 2 (the factor is already included) gives −0.09 V.

q: When a lead storage battery is being recharged, which reaction takes place at the positive plate?
x: Charging reverses discharge: at the positive plate (PbO₂ plate) PbSO₄ is oxidised back to PbO₂, which releases electrons. The reduction of PbSO₄ to Pb happens at the negative plate, and PbO₂ → PbSO₄ is the discharge reaction, the tempting reversal.

q: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell delivers 0.4 F of charge. What mass of water is produced? (H = 1, O = 16)
x: Each H₂ gives 2 electrons (H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻) and forms one H₂O, so 0.4 F → 0.2 mol H₂ → 0.2 mol H₂O = 3.6 g. Taking one electron per water molecule gives 7.2 g.
